This tutorial has no lecture notes. The page follows the acid–base workshop slides (black), then every acid–base and electrolyte question from the gifts of all lectures (red). Practice-case answers were not on the slides — the worked answers below are marked (added).

Objective

  • To provide a simple, systematic approach to interpreting arterial blood gas (ABG) samples.
  • Multiple formulas and rules exist, but all that is needed is a little clinical information from the history and examination, a few readily available lab tests, and the knowledge of five simple steps.
  • Doing these steps on every patient with an ABG and electrolytes decreases missed complex (mixed) acid–base disturbances.

The five steps

StepQuestionHow
1Acidemia or alkalemia?pH < 7.38 = acidemia · pH > 7.42 = alkalemia
2Primary respiratory or metabolic?Look at PCO₂ and pH: same direction → metabolic; opposite directions → respiratory
3Is compensation appropriate?Use the four compensation rules below
4Is there an anion-gap metabolic acidosis (AGMA)?AG = Na − (HCO₃ + Cl); > 12 → AGMA
5If metabolic acidosis — another metabolic disorder too?AGMA → Δgap; NAGMA → Cl vs HCO₃ rule

Step 2 — which primary disorder?

DisorderpHPCO₂HCO₃
Metabolic acidosis↓↓ (compensation)↓ (primary)
Respiratory acidosis↓↑ (primary)↑ (compensation)
Metabolic alkalosis↑↑ (compensation)↑ (primary)
Respiratory alkalosis↑↓ (primary)↓ (compensation)
Trick: if pH and PCO₂ move in the same direction → metabolic. If they move in opposite directions → respiratory.

Step 3 — expected compensation

Primary disorderExpected compensation
Metabolic acidosisPCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃ + 8 (± 2) (Winter's formula)
Metabolic alkalosis↑PCO₂ = 0.6 × ↑HCO₃ (± 2)
Respiratory acidosisFor every ↑PCO₂ 10 → HCO₃ ↑ 1 (acute) or ↑ 4 (chronic)
Respiratory alkalosisFor every ↓PCO₂ 10 → HCO₃ ↓ 2 (acute) or ↓ 5 (chronic)
  • If the measured PCO₂ is higher than expected in metabolic acidosis → an added respiratory acidosis; lower than expected → an added respiratory alkalosis.

Step 4 — anion gap

  • AG = Na − (Cl + HCO₃). Sodium is the only significant measured cation; the measured anions are chloride and bicarbonate. Normal ≈ 12.
  • Low albumin pitfall: albumin carries negative charges, so with low albumin the "normal" AG is lower. For every 1 g/dL drop in albumin, AG falls by 2.5. Example: calculated AG 10 with a 2 g drop in albumin → corrected AG 15 = a hidden AGMA.
  • AG = Na − (Cl + HCO₃): Na 132, Cl 95, HCO₃ 15 → 22 431 438 Final; Na 132, Cl 95, HCO₃ 8 → 29 432; Na 126, Cl 90, HCO₃ 11 → 25. 434 ×2

Step 5 — a second metabolic disorder?

  • If AGMA → Δgap = ΔAG − ΔHCO₃ = (AG − 12) − (24 − HCO₃).
    • Between −6 and +6 → no other metabolic disorder.
    • > +6 → AGMA + metabolic alkalosis.
    • < −6 → AGMA + non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA).
  • If NAGMA → for every 1 mEq/L ↑ in Cl, HCO₃ should fall by 1 mEq/L (± 5). If HCO₃ falls less than predicted → NAGMA + metabolic alkalosis.

Metabolic acidosis

  • With pH < 7.38, metabolic acidosis is the primary disorder when the PCO₂ is < 40 or the HCO₃ is < 24. It is classified by the anion gap.
  • Detecting an AGMA matters because only a few conditions cause it, and in mixed disorders a raised AG may be the only clue that a metabolic acidosis is present.

Anion-gap metabolic acidosis (AGMA)

  • Four main groups: renal failure, ketoacidosis, toxins, lactic acidosis.
A CAT MUDPILES
AnalgesicsMassive NSAID, acetaminophen
Cyanide, Carbon monoxide
Arsenic, Alcoholic ketoacidosis
Toluene
Methanol, Metformin
Uremia
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Paraldehyde, Phenformin
Iron, Isoniazid
Lactic acidosise.g. shock, haemorrhage, ischaemic bowel
Ethylene glycol
Salicylates
  • Osmol gap: in any AGMA, calculate an osmol gap — a clue to life-threatening toxic alcohol ingestion (ethylene glycol, methanol). Osmol gap = measured − calculated osmolality. Calculated osmolality = 2(Na) + Glucose/18 + BUN/2.4 + EtOH/4.6.

Worked example (slides) — methanol

  • 32-year-old man, depression and alcohol abuse, altered mental status. pH 6.9, PCO₂ 29, PO₂ 100; Na 140, Cl 101, HCO₃ 5.
  • Step 1 acidosis · Step 2 metabolic · Step 3 expected PCO₂ = 1.5(5) + 8 = 15, but measured 29 → respiratory acidosis too (CNS depression).
  • Step 4 AG = 140 − (101 + 5) = 34 · Step 5 Δgap = (34 − 12) − (24 − 5) = 3 → no other metabolic disorder.
  • Answer: AGMA + respiratory acidosis. Osmol gap 174, methanol level 510 mg/dL.
  • High-AG acidosis cause → severe haemorrhage (shock → lactic acidosis). Diarrhoea, intestinal fistula and hyperchloraemic acidosis are normal-AG. 432 ×2
  • ICU septic shock with sudden abdominal pain, distension and lactic acidosis → non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia. 442 Final
  • "Triad of death" in trauma = acidosis, hypothermia and coagulopathy. 439

Non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA)

  • Due to GI or renal loss of bicarbonate.
  • GI vs renal can be separated with urine electrolytes: urine anion gap = Na + K − Cl. An excess of negative ions (negative urine AG) → GI loss; a positive urine AG → the acidaemia is due to the kidney (e.g. RTA).
  • Normal-AG metabolic acidosis: small-intestinal fistula 437; cause → renal tubular acidosis ("hyperchloraemic acidosis" is a description, not a cause; lactic acidosis and DKA are high-AG). 431
  • High ileostomy output → non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (loss of bicarbonate-rich small-bowel fluid). 441
  • Small-bowel / enterocutaneous fistula → metabolic acidosis. 439 432 ×3

Worked example (slides) — diarrhoea

  • 68-year-old man after antibiotics, 10 watery stools/day for 5 days. pH 7.34, PCO₂ 34, PO₂ 80; Na 135, Cl 108, HCO₃ 18.
  • Acidosis · metabolic · expected PCO₂ = 1.5(18) + 8 = 35 (appropriate) · AG = 135 − (108 + 18) = 9 (normal) · Cl ↑ by 8 and HCO₃ ↓ by 6 → no metabolic alkalosis.
  • Answer: NAGMA due to diarrhoea.

Respiratory acidosis

  • ↑PCO₂ and ↓pH, most commonly from hypoventilation — the lungs can't excrete CO₂ as fast as the body makes it.
Cause groupExamples
CNS depressionSedatives/opioids, CNS disease, sleep apnoea
Pleural diseaseLarge pneumothorax, pleural effusion
Lung diseaseARDS, COPD, pulmonary oedema, severe pneumonia
Acute airway obstructionLaryngospasm, sleep apnoea
NeuromuscularGuillain–Barré, myasthenia gravis, botulism
Thoracic cage injuryFlail chest
Ventilator dysfunction
  • The kidney compensates by retaining bicarbonate over hours to days (maximal by ~4 days), so the HCO₃ rise tells you how long it has been going on.
  • pH rule: acute → pH falls 0.08 per 10 mmHg ↑PCO₂; chronic → pH falls 0.03 per 10 mmHg.
  • Telling acute from chronic matters: an acute rise warns of a patient spiralling down who may need emergent intubation; a chronic retainer is in less immediate danger.

Worked example (slides) — COPD

  • 70-year-old smoker, acute shortness of breath. pH 7.30, PCO₂ 60, PO₂ 60; Na 135, Cl 100, HCO₃ 30.
  • Acidosis · respiratory · PCO₂ ↑20 → HCO₃ should rise 2 if acute, 8 if chronic; it rose 6 → acute-on-chronic.
  • AG = 135 − (100 + 30) = 5 → no AGMA. (The slide printed 100 + 26 = 9; either way, no AGMA.)
  • Answer: acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis (COPD exacerbation).
  • Excess opiates after gastrectomy, pH 7.3 → high PaCO₂ (respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation). 431 ×3
  • Emphysema + haematemesis, confused, pH 7.23, PO₂ 42, PCO₂ 75 → endotracheal intubation and ventilation 430 ×2; the 426 version keyed correct hypoxia with oxygen. 426
  • Chest trauma, agitated, hypotensive, reduced air entry on one side, pH 7.3, PaCO₂ 52, SaO₂ 80 → needle decompression (tension pneumothorax — breathing problem first). 434 ×2 Mid+Final
  • Early-morning headache in raised ICP → ↑ systemic PCO₂ (hypoventilation during sleep → cerebral vasodilation). 434 Final ×2
  • Hyperventilation lowers ICP by cerebral vasoconstriction (low PCO₂) — a temporary measure only. 434 ×2

Metabolic alkalosis

  • ↑ serum bicarbonate. Causes:
    • Volume contraction — vomiting, NG suction, loop or thiazide diuretics.
    • Excess glucocorticoids or mineralocorticoids (e.g. Cushing's).
    • Hypokalaemia.
    • Bartter's syndrome.
    • Alkali ingestion/infusion.
    • Post-hypercapnic alkalosis.
  • Urine chloride separates volume depletion (the commonest cause) from the rest:
Urine ClTypeCause
< 10Saline-responsiveVolume depletion (vomiting, NG suction)
> 10Saline-resistantOther causes (mineralocorticoid excess, etc.)

Worked example (slides) — vomiting

  • 20-year-old student, excessive vomiting after binge drinking. pH 7.50, PCO₂ 44, PO₂ 100; Na 138, Cl 100, HCO₃ 30.
  • Alkalosis · metabolic · expected ↑PCO₂ = 0.6 × 6 = 3.6; measured ↑4 → appropriate · AG = 138 − (100 + 30) = 8.
  • Answer: metabolic alkalosis secondary to vomiting.
  • Metabolic alkalosis = loss of fixed acid or gain of bicarbonate (compensated by hypo-, not hyper-ventilation). 437
  • Vomiting / gastric outlet obstruction / NG suction → hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis: NGT after cholecystectomy 438 ×4; chronic DU with vomiting of old food 434 ×2; prepyloric ulcer with vomiting 432 431 ×6; NGT after hemicolectomy, pH 7.5, high HCO₃ → hypokalaemia. 432 ×4
  • Gastric fistula after sleeve gastrectomy (250 mL/day) → hypokalaemia. 435 ×7 435 ×7

Respiratory alkalosis

  • ↓PCO₂ and ↑pH. The PO₂ helps separate lung disease (low PO₂) from other causes of hyperpnoea (e.g. fever).
  • Causes: CNS disease (CVA), toxins (salicylates), high altitude, severe anaemia, pregnancy, lung disease/hypoxia (asthma, pneumonia, PE, pulmonary oedema, fibrosis), anxiety, cirrhosis, fever/sepsis, ventilator dysfunction.

Worked example (slides) — anxiety

  • 22-year-old woman, 4 hours of numbness in both hands like previous anxiety episodes. pH 7.48, PCO₂ 30, PO₂ 86; Na 140, Cl 110, HCO₃ 22.
  • Alkalosis · respiratory · PCO₂ ↓10 → HCO₃ ↓2 if acute, 5 if chronic; it fell 2 → acute · AG = 140 − (110 + 22) = 8.
  • Answer: acute respiratory alkalosis (panic attack).
  • pH 7.5, PCO₂ 25, HCO₃ 24 → respiratory alkalosis. 442

Electrolytes & resuscitation (from past exams)

  • The most common fluid problem in surgical patients → extracellular (volume) losses. 437
  • Most accurate indicator of inadequate tissue perfusion in a hypotensive trauma patient → serum lactate 438 ×2; most accurate indicator of adequate fluid replacement → urine output. 434 ×4
  • Hyperchloraemic acidosis after crystalloids + blood in a head-injured patient (Cl 115, HCO₃ 13) → keyed Ringer's lactate bolus (avoid more normal saline). 430
  • Hyperkalaemia emergency (K 6.9 in CKD) → calcium (chloride/gluconate) first to protect the heart. 429
  • Hypocalcaemia with prolonged QT → IV calcium gluconate. 439
  • Massive transfusion → hyperkalaemia 431 ×2 and citrate toxicity (hypocalcaemia). 426
  • Reperfusion after revascularising an acutely ischaemic limb → hyperkalaemia (also acidosis, myoglobinuria). 436 Final
  • Rising urea/creatinine on gentamicin → stop gentamicin. 431 ×2

Practice cases (slides) — worked answers (added)

Added explanationThe slides list these 8 cases without answers. Each answer below uses the five steps exactly as taught. Try each case first, then tap Show the worked answer.

Case 1

  • 40-year-old man with abdominal pain. pH 7.42; PCO₂ 33; Na 141; Cl 90; HCO₃ 24.
Show the worked answer
AddedpH normal but AG = 141 − (90 + 24) = 27 → AGMA. Δgap = (27 − 12) − (24 − 24) = 15 (> 6) → + metabolic alkalosis. Expected PCO₂ for HCO₃ 24 ≈ 44, measured 33 → + respiratory alkalosis. A triple disorder hiding behind a normal pH.

Case 2

  • Chronic alcoholic with vomiting and abdominal pain. Na 137, K 3.8, Cl 90, pH 7.40, PCO₂ 41, HCO₃ 22.
Show the worked answer
AddedAG = 137 − (90 + 22) = 25 → AGMA (alcoholic ketoacidosis). Δgap = 13 − 2 = 11 → + metabolic alkalosis (vomiting). Expected PCO₂ = 1.5(22) + 8 = 41 → appropriate.

Case 3

  • Diabetic with diarrhoea and cough; CXR infiltrate. pH 7.31; PCO₂ 10; Na 123; Cl 99; HCO₃ 5.
Show the worked answer
Addedacidosis, metabolic. AG = 123 − (99 + 5) = 19 → AGMA (DKA). Expected PCO₂ = 1.5(5) + 8 = 15.5 ± 2, measured 10 → + respiratory alkalosis (pneumonia). Δgap = 7 − 19 = −12 → + NAGMA (diarrhoea).

Case 4

  • Alcoholic with vomiting. pH 7.20; PCO₂ 25; Na 130; Cl 80; HCO₃ 10.
Show the worked answer
Addedacidosis, metabolic. Expected PCO₂ = 1.5(10) + 8 = 23 ± 2 → 25 is appropriate. AG = 130 − (80 + 10) = 40 → AGMA (ketoacidosis). Δgap = 28 − 14 = 14 → + metabolic alkalosis (vomiting).

Case 5

  • Man with arthritis: confusion, shortness of breath, sweating. pH 7.30; PCO₂ 18; Na 147; Cl 108; HCO₃ 16.
Show the worked answer
Addedacidosis, metabolic. AG = 147 − (108 + 16) = 23 → AGMA. Expected PCO₂ = 1.5(16) + 8 = 32, measured 18 → + respiratory alkalosis. Δgap = 11 − 8 = 3 → nothing else. Classic salicylate (aspirin) toxicity.

Case 6

  • COPD patient, short of breath. pH 7.18; PCO₂ 80; Na 135; Cl 93; HCO₃ 30.
Show the worked answer
Addedacidosis, respiratory. PCO₂ ↑40 → HCO₃ should rise 4 (acute) or 16 (chronic); it rose 6 → acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis. AG = 135 − (93 + 30) = 12 → no AGMA.

Case 7

  • Woman with Crohn's: fever, vomiting, diarrhoea. pH 7.36; PCO₂ 22; Na 147; Cl 121; HCO₃ 14.
Show the worked answer
AddedAG = 147 − (121 + 14) = 12 → NAGMA (diarrhoea). Expected PCO₂ = 1.5(14) + 8 = 29 ± 2, measured 22 → + respiratory alkalosis (fever). Cl ↑21 but HCO₃ ↓ only 10 (less than predicted) → + metabolic alkalosis (vomiting).

Case 8

  • Non-compliant diabetic with cirrhosis, vomiting. pH 7.46; PCO₂ 17; Na 133; Cl 84; HCO₃ 15.
Show the worked answer
Addedalkalaemia with low PCO₂ → respiratory alkalosis (cirrhosis). AG = 133 − (84 + 15) = 34 → + AGMA (DKA). Δgap = 22 − 9 = 13 → + metabolic alkalosis (vomiting).

• Severe hypophosphatemia is a medical emergency requiring IV sodium phosphate (Na₂PO₄) or potassium phosphate (K₂PO₄) based on the patient’s electrolyte profile.
    • Mild cases can be treated with oral phosphate supplements or phosphate-rich foods (e.g., milk).
Hyperphosphatemia
  • Etiology
    • Hyperphosphatemia is uncommon in surgical patients but can occur in:
    • Severe renal disease (impaired phosphate excretion)
    • Severe trauma (tissue breakdown releasing phosphate)
  • Presentation
    • Usually asymptomatic
    • Can cause hypocalcemia due to calcium phosphate precipitation and tissue deposition
  • Treatment
    • Diuresis to enhance phosphate excretion
    • Phosphate binders (e.g., aluminum hydroxide) to reduce intestinal absorption
    • Hemodialysis for severe cases or renal failure
  • Acid-base disorders
Metabolic acidosis
  • Etiology
    • Increased production of H⁺ (acid overload)
    • Excessive loss of HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate loss)
  • Common causes in surgical patients:
    • Trauma, critically ill, and postoperative patients
    • Shock (most common surgical cause due to lactic acidosis)
  • Anion Gap (AG) in Metabolic Acidosis
    • The serum anion gap (AG) helps differentiate causes of metabolic acidosis:
    • AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3)
  • Normal AG (<12): Metabolic acidosis due to bicarbonate loss
    • Causes: Diarrhea, high small-bowel output (e.g., ileostomy), renal tubular acidosis, iatrogenic hyperchloremia from large- volume normal saline administration
  • Increased AG (>12): Metabolic acidosis due to acid accumulation
    • Causes (MUDPILES mnemonic):
    • Methanol ingestion
    • Uremia (renal failure)
    • Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
    • Propylene glycol ingestion
    • Isoniazid toxicity
    • Lactic acidosis (most common in surgical patients, often from shock/sepsis)
    • Ethylene glycol ingestion
    • Salicylate poisoning
  • Treatment
    • Identify and correct the underlying cause (e.g., sepsis, shock, diarrhea, renal failure).
    • Bicarbonate replacement (NaHCO₃⁻) is often unnecessary unless the patient has severe metabolic acidosis with renal dysfunction.
    • Chronic metabolic acidosis (e.g., in chronic renal failure): Managed with oral NaHCO₃⁻ and strategies to minimize bicarbonate loss.
  • Compensation
    • The body compensates for metabolic acidosis by respiratory hyperventilation (blowing off CO₂).
    • Winter’s formula estimates expected pCO₂ compensation: pCO2 = (1.5×HCO3) + (8±2)
    • If pCO₂ is outside this range, an additional acid-base disorder is present.
Metabolic alkalosis
  • Etiology
    • Metabolic alkalosis in surgical patients is commonly caused by:
    • Loss of H⁺ (gastric losses) → Vomiting, gastric suctioning, or drainage
    • Hypovolemia → Leads to renal compensation that retains bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)
    • Total body potassium (K⁺) depletion → Often due to diuretics or renal failure
  • Presentation
    • Hypokalemia symptoms: Muscle weakness, arrhythmias
    • Hypocalcemia symptoms: Tetany, seizures
    • Urine findings:
    • Low Na⁺, K⁺, and Cl⁻
    • Acidic urine in paradoxical aciduria
    • Alkaline urine in simple volume depletion
  • Treatment
    • Fluid repletion (IV normal saline) → Restores volume and enhances HCO₃⁻ excretion.
    • Potassium replacement (KCl) → Prevents life-threatening hypokalemia and corrects alkalosis.
    • Chloride replacement (Cl⁻ from NaCl or KCl) → Allows for Na⁺ and K⁺ reabsorption with Cl⁻ instead of HCO₃⁻.
    • Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) → Enhances renal bicarbonate excretion in euvolemic patients.
    • Severe alkalosis: IV HCl may be required.
  • Compensation
    • Respiratory compensation: The body retains CO₂ (hypoventilation), increasing pCO₂ by ~0.7 mmHg for every 1 mmol/L rise in HCO₃⁻.
    • pCO₂ rarely exceeds 55 mmHg.
    • pCO₂ > 60 mmHg suggests coexisting respiratory acidosis.
Respiratory acidosis
  • Etiology
    • Acute respiratory acidosis occurs when ventilation is impaired, leading to CO₂ accumulation and subsequent conversion to carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), causing acidosis.
  • Common causes in surgical patients include:
    • Impaired gas exchange leading to hypoventilation:
    • Respiratory arrest, acute airway obstruction
    • Pulmonary edema, pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
    • Saddle pulmonary embolus, aspiration of intraoral contents
    • Postoperative hypoventilation:
    • Oversedation (narcotics, benzodiazepines, or residual anesthesia effects)
    • Pain-induced respiratory splinting (e.g., abdominal incisions, rib fractures)
    • CNS causes:
    • Head trauma (direct brainstem injury or herniation)
    • Excess ethanol ingestion (decreases respiratory drive)
    • Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) & obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) → May lead to chronic respiratory acidosis with some renal compensation.
    • Chronic respiratory acidosis: Seen in chronic respiratory failure (e.g., COPD).
  • Treatment
    • Pulmonary therapy & supportive care:
    • Chest physiotherapy & pulmonary toilet for post- surgical patients
    • Diuretics for pulmonary edema
    • Antibiotics for pneumonia
    • Reversal of sedation:
    • Naloxone (opioid overdose)
    • Flumazenil (benzodiazepine overdose)
    • Mechanical ventilation (intubation) if necessary to correct pCO₂.
  • Caution:
    • Too-rapid correction of chronic respiratory acidosis can cause post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis, leading to:
    • Muscle spasms
    • Potentially fatal cardiac arrhythmias
  • Compensation
    • For every 10 mmHg increase in pCO₂, HCO₃⁻ should increase by ~1mmol/L (adequate compensation).
Respiratory alkalosis
  • Etiology
    • Respiratory alkalosis occurs due to hyperventilation, which lowers pCO₂ (hypocapnia), leading to alkalosis.
  • Common causes in surgical patients include:
    • Anxiety, agitation, pain (most common postoperative causes)
    • Early signs of sepsis
    • Moderate pulmonary embolism
    • Chronic causes: Chronic pulmonary or liver disease
  • Treatment
    • Address the underlying cause:
    • Pain control
    • Sedation or anxiolytics (if anxiety-induced)
    • Mechanical ventilation with paralysis (if severe and necessary)
  • Chronic respiratory alkalosis:
    • Does not require treatment if well-compensated.
    • Rapid correction can cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, which can be severe.
  • Compensation
    • Adequate renal compensation:
    • For every 10 mmHg decrease in pCO₂, HCO₃⁻ should decrease by ~2 mmol/L.
Mixed acid-base disorders
  • Mixed acid-base disorders occur when compensatory changes are either inadequate or exaggerated, leading to a normal or near-normal pH despite abnormal bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) and carbon dioxide (pCO₂) levels.
  • Steps to identify mixed disorders:
  • 1. Determine the primary acid-base disorder (metabolic vs. respiratory, acidosis vs. alkalosis).
  • 2. Assess whether compensation is appropriate using standard formulas.
    • Inadequate or excessive compensation indicates a mixed disorder.
  • 3. For metabolic acidosis, calculate the anion gap (AG): AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3)
  • 4. Perform the Delta-Delta (Δ-Δ) calculation to detect additional metabolic disorders: ΔΔ = (AG − 12) / (24 − HCO3)
    • ΔΔ < 1: Indicates both AG metabolic acidosis and non-AG metabolic acidosis (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis with renal bicarbonate loss).
    • ΔΔ > 1: Suggests AG metabolic acidosis with metabolic alkalosis (e.g., septic patients on diuretics or gastric suction).
  • Common Mixed Acid-Base Disorders in Surgery
    • Metabolic acidosis + respiratory alkalosis (Most common in surgical patients):
    • Seen in septic shock, hepatorenal syndrome, and salicylate poisoning.
    • pH may appear normal due to opposing effects on H⁺ balance.
    • Mixed respiratory acidosis + metabolic alkalosis (Less common, but serious):
    • Occurs in cardiorespiratory arrest (a medical emergency).
  • Diagnosis & Management
    • Correct the underlying causes (e.g., sepsis, renal failure, respiratory failure).
    • Address electrolyte imbalances (e.g., K⁺, Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻) to restore acid-base homeostasis.
